opus-5.5.text:
I think there's actually a lot of scope, and it's one of the areas I'm most excited about people outside the labs getting involved in.

A big part of it is that evaluations are, in some ways, more accessible than a lot of other safety work. You don't necessarily need access to the model weights or a giant compute budget to do something useful. If you're a domain expert — say, in biology, or cybersecurity, or some specialized area of chemistry — you often understand far better than we do what a genuinely dangerous capability would look like. What's the step that's actually hard? What's the knowledge that's the real bottleneck versus the stuff that's already in a textbook? Turning that expertise into a concrete test that tells you whether a model has crossed a meaningful line is incredibly valuable, and it's hard for any single lab to have that depth across every domain.

Then there's the methodological side. Building good evals is genuinely difficult. You want them to be hard enough that they don't saturate immediately, you want them to measure the thing you actually care about rather than some proxy, and you want to be confident you're eliciting the model's full capabilities rather than underestimating it because you prompted it badly. People in academia or at independent organizations can make real progress on those questions — things like how to do elicitation well, how to think about scaffolding and agents, how to avoid contamination.

There's also an important role for third-party evaluators and government bodies like the AI safety institutes. If the only people checking whether a model is dangerous are the people who built it, that's a weaker system than one where there's external verification. So I'd like to see that ecosystem grow — organizations that can test models before deployment, check the labs' claims, and push back when they disagree.

And honestly, part of the reason this matters is that our responsible scaling policy depends on having good evals. The commitments are only as meaningful as our ability to tell whether a model has hit a given capability threshold. So if people outside are building better ways to measure that, it directly strengthens the whole framework — not just for us, but hopefully for the industry more broadly.

r001.rationale: The response discusses eliciting a model’s capabilities as an evaluation challenge, but does not say this must happen internally at the AI developer.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says people outside the labs can contribute and describes domain experts and independent organizations building evaluations.

r003.rationale: It does not identify proposing new AI-risk categories as an outside contribution.

r004.rationale: It does not identify developing AI threat models as an outside contribution.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there's actually a lot of scope, and probably more than people assume. There's a tendency to think that because the frontier models live inside a handful of labs, all the meaningful evaluation work has to happen inside those labs too. I don't think that's right.

A few reasons. First, the models are accessible. You can get API access to Claude or GPT or Gemini, and a huge amount of evaluation work is really just: design a careful test, run the model against it many times, and analyze what you see. You don't need weights for that. Some of the best eval work I've seen on things like sandbagging, situational awareness, or long-horizon agentic tasks has come from outside groups like METR, Apollo, or academic labs, who had nothing but API access and a lot of care in experimental design.

Second, I'd say the bottleneck isn't really compute or model access, it's good ideas and good execution. Evaluations are hard to build well. It's very easy to write a benchmark that looks like it measures something dangerous and then discover the model is just pattern-matching on the format, or that the threshold you picked doesn't actually map to real-world harm. Figuring out what "concerning capability" means concretely enough that you could measure it, and then validating that your measurement tracks the thing you care about, is genuinely difficult intellectual work, and a lot of it is domain knowledge the labs don't have in house. If you're a biosecurity expert or a cybersecurity person, you probably understand the real-world uplift question better than most ML researchers do.

Third, there's a credibility argument. When we publish our own evaluations of our own models, people reasonably ask whether we're grading our own homework. Independent evaluators, and eventually government bodies like the AI safety institutes, are important partly because they don't have our incentives. For something like a Responsible Scaling Policy to mean much, you want external parties who can check whether the claims hold up.

Where I'd temper it slightly: there are some things that are harder from outside. Interpretability on the frontier models mostly requires weights. Red-teaming the actual deployment, with all the safeguards layered on, requires cooperation from the lab. And evaluating pre-release models obviously requires the lab to give you access, which is why building trusted relationships with external evaluators matters so much.

But if someone asked me "should I go do evals work outside a lab, or is that a waste of time," I'd say it's clearly not a waste. If anything, I'd like there to be a lot more of it. We're not going to be able to do all of this ourselves, and honestly we shouldn't be the only ones doing it.

r001.rationale: The response says substantial evaluation work can happen outside labs and explicitly rejects the idea that meaningful work must happen internally.

r002.rationale: It says external groups can design and run evaluations using API access, and that work outside a lab is clearly worthwhile.

r003.rationale: It discusses designing tests and evaluating named risks, but does not identify proposing new AI-risk categories as an external contribution.

r004.rationale: It discusses domain expertise and real-world uplift, but does not identify developing AI threat models as an external contribution.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of scope. Evaluating AI risks is a much bigger problem than any one company can handle, and people outside the company can bring expertise and perspectives that we don’t have internally.

One useful contribution is developing evaluations that actually tell us something about risk. There’s a gap between showing that a model can answer questions about a dangerous topic and showing that it could materially help someone do something harmful. Designing tests that get at that distinction is hard. It often requires domain expertise, as well as an understanding of how people use these systems.

Independent scrutiny is also valuable. We should want people to challenge the assumptions behind our evaluations, identify things we’ve missed, and ask whether the evidence supports our conclusions.

The constraint is that some of this work requires access to models or information that isn’t publicly available. So there’s a responsibility on companies to make meaningful external evaluation possible. But there’s also useful work people can do with publicly available models: developing methods, testing how robust an evaluation is, and showing where existing tests fail. That can give us a much better foundation for evaluating more capable systems.

r001.rationale: The response notes that some evaluation work needs access to nonpublic models or information, but does not say capability elicitation must happen internally at the developer.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes developing risk evaluations as a useful contribution and says people outside the company can do useful evaluation work.

r003.rationale: It does not identify proposing new AI-risk categories as an outside contribution.

r004.rationale: It does not identify developing AI threat models as an outside contribution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of scope. One thing that’s useful is to distinguish between developing an evaluation and running it on a particular model. Running it might require access that’s difficult to get from outside a lab. But coming up with a good way to test for a dangerous capability, and understanding what the results would actually tell us, is work that people outside the lab can contribute to.

For example, if you’re worried about models helping with some particular kind of harmful activity, you need people who understand that domain to work out what tasks would be meaningful tests. Can the model do something that would otherwise be a real bottleneck? Are we measuring something consequential, or just whether it can answer questions about the topic?

There’s also a valuable independent role in scrutinising the evaluations themselves. What are they missing? How much reassurance should a passing result give us? I’d like there to be a much broader community working on those questions, because the labs shouldn’t be the only people deciding whether their own evidence is convincing.

r001.rationale: It says running an evaluation may require access that is difficult to get from outside a lab, but does not state capability elicitation must happen internally at the developer.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says people outside the lab can develop good ways to test dangerous capabilities and assess what results would show.

r003.rationale: It discusses testing harmful activities but does not identify proposing new AI-risk categories as an outside contribution.

r004.rationale: It does not identify developing AI threat models as an outside contribution.
